grid_world_pain · simulation study · recovery tuning

Making rest in the open not worth taking

Which healing settings leave an injured agent unable to recover anywhere except inside a bush — and why the two settings that ship today do the opposite.

PURPOSE

In this simulation an animal walks a grid, eats, gets hurt, and heals only by choosing the Rest action. Injury is a number from 0 to 100; at 100 the animal dies. Some grid squares hold a bush, which hides the animal from a hunting predator and which predators cannot walk into. A setting called body.recovery_in_bush_multiplier can make resting inside a bush heal faster than resting on open ground. It ships at 1, meaning “no difference at all”.

This page asks a tuning question: what values of the healing settings would make resting out in the open not worth doing at all, so that an injured animal has to travel to cover to get better? That is a design goal, not a fact about the world — the point of making cover the only place to heal is to see whether an animal that is hurt starts using cover, which is a behaviour this project wants to be able to study.

The answer. Set the open-ground healing rate to recovery_base_rate: 0.2, switch the compounding off with recovery_accel_rate: 0, and set recovery_in_bush_multiplier: 25. An animal that rests in the open for every step it can afford clears 10 injury points; the same animal resting in a bush closes a bad 70-point wound in 14 rest steps. Both shipped settings fail badly: each of them clears the entire 100-point injury scale out in the open, one in 15.3 rest steps.

01 What a reader needs before the figures

Everything below refers to one simulation. A short inventory, because none of it is guessable from the figures.

step
One environment timestep. An episode runs at most 500 steps. In every figure the t = 0 row is the initial state, not a step.
injury_level
The body variable this study is about, on a 0–100 scale. Reaching 100 ends the episode.
Rest
One of the agent's actions. It is the only way injury ever goes down. A resting agent does not move and does not eat.
nutrition
The hunger variable, also 0–100. It falls by metabolic_cost = 1 every single step; reaching 0 ends the episode by starvation.
bush
An obstacle carrying hides_agent: true. It conceals the agent from a hunting predator, and since 2026-09-14 also blocks animals from entering the cell. It is the “cover” this page keeps referring to.
recovery_base_rate
Injury points healed on the first rest step of a streak.
recovery_accel_rate
How much more each consecutive rest step heals than the one before it, as a fraction. At 0 the healing rate is flat; at 0.5 each step heals 1.5× the last.
recovery_in_bush_multiplier
What the healing is multiplied by on a step the agent rests while standing on a bush. Must be greater than 0. At exactly 1.0 the whole mechanism is not even compiled into the simulation.
nociception
The signal the agent receives about its injury. This page does not use it — the study is about the body variable, not about what the agent can feel.

02 The definition the study turns on

Definition

Resting outside cover is “not meaningfully recoverable” when an agent that rests continuously in the open for its entire affordable rest budget cannot clear more than θ of the injury scale.

The affordable rest budget is nutrition / metabolic_cost, because a resting agent eats nothing, so nutrition — not injury — is what bounds how long it can go on resting.

This page uses θ = 25 injury points of 100 and a 50-step budget as the primary setting. Both are choices, not facts. §10 shows what moves if either changes, and §11 records where those choices turned out to need qualifying.

Two sentences on why those numbers and not others. 25 points is a quarter of the scale and is roughly the smallest single hit a predator can land on the jump-attack world, whose per-hit damage is drawn from 15 to 120 — so “cannot clear θ” means “cannot undo even a glancing blow”. 50 steps is the median of a start nutrition drawn uniformly from 0 to 100 at a metabolic_cost of 1, which is the draw the random-init worlds use.

The complementary requirement

A world in which nobody can heal is not the goal. So a second condition has to hold at the same time: cover must be usable — an agent resting in a bush should clear a typical 70-point wound within about 25 rest steps. The two conditions pull in opposite directions, and the whole tuning problem is the gap between them.

Throughout, condition A means the first (the open must not heal) and condition B the second (cover must heal).

03 The arithmetic, as the simulation actually computes it

Five lines, transcribed from src/environment/core.py lines 226-266. Everything on this page is derived from them in code; no cumulative total anywhere is typed by hand.

← the code is wider than the box — scroll it sideways

# streak counts CONSECUTIVE rest steps; any non-rest step resets it to 0
streak(t)       = rested ? streak(t-1) + 1 : 0
recovery_amount = recovery_base_rate * (1 + recovery_accel_rate) ** (max(streak,1) - 1)
# the location premium multiplies the AMOUNT, so it inherits the two conditions below
if recovery_in_bush_multiplier != 1.0 and in_bush:  recovery_amount *= multiplier
can_recover     = rested AND applied_inc <= 0
new_injury      = clip(injury + applied_inc - recovery_amount * can_recover, 0, max_injury)

Two consequences do all the work. Because the streak is 1 on the first rest step and the exponent is streak -⁠ 1, the heal on the n-th consecutive rest step is base × (1 + accel)^(n-⁠1). The cumulative heal over n steps is therefore a geometric sum:

cumulative(n) = base × n   when accel = 0,   and   base × ((1 + accel)n − 1) / accel   otherwise  —  times the multiplier, in cover.

Rearranged, the two conditions become almost embarrassingly simple at recovery_accel_rate = 0. Condition A is base ≤ θ / budget, which is 0.5 at the primary setting. Condition B is base × multiplier ≥ wound / cover steps, which is 2.8 injury points per rest step. Notice that A depends on θ and the budget only through their ratio — halving the threshold and doubling the budget are the same move, which is why one set of lines in Figure 3 carries both sensitivities.

04 Two shipped settings, two different problems

Why this analysis

Two recovery settings exist in the repository and it is tempting to treat them as two points on one dial. They are not. One compounds and one does not, and the difference decides whether “how much can the open heal?” even has a bounded answer. An informative figure here would show the compounding curve leaving the flat one behind fast enough that no single base rate can stand in for both.

05 Where the open is already unrecoverable

Why this analysis

Condition A is a statement about a single number: how much injury a continuously-resting agent can clear outside cover before it starves. Figure 1 evaluates that number at three points; this figure evaluates it everywhere in the plane that any shipped configuration occupies, and draws the line where it equals θ. An informative answer tells us whether the workable region is a large comfortable area or a sliver — and therefore whether the recommendation is robust or delicately balanced.

06 The answer figure: where both conditions hold

Why this analysis

This is the figure the study exists to produce. Condition A caps the base rate; condition B puts a floor under the base rate times the multiplier. Plotted against each other, the settings that satisfy both form a region, and the tuning question becomes “which point in that region?” rather than “does one exist?”. An informative answer would show a region with room in it — a single feasible point would mean the design was balanced on a knife edge and would break the first time somebody edited a threshold.

07 Does any compounding at all survive?

Why this analysis

Figure 3 fixes recovery_accel_rate at zero, and a fixed parameter is an assumption until something tests it. The worry is specific: compounding is exactly the mechanism that lets a tiny base rate clear a large wound if the agent simply keeps resting, so a small positive acceleration might quietly undo condition A. An informative answer is a number — the largest acceleration each base rate can tolerate — not a yes or a no.

08 The check that the algebra is the simulation

Why this analysis

Figures 1 to 4 are all the same closed form, transcribed by hand from the simulation's source. If that transcription is wrong, four figures are confidently wrong together and nothing else on this page would show it. So this figure drives the real environment with a scripted always-Rest policy, once with the agent standing on a bush and once on bare ground, and plots what the simulation actually did against what the formula predicted. Agreement validates the algebra. Disagreement would mean the algebra is wrong, and the honest response would be to say so rather than adjust the plot.

Validation result

Agreement. Over 102 compared values the largest disagreement between the simulation and the closed form is 1.53e-04 injury points, which is single-precision rounding accumulated over 50 steps — the smallest representable gap near injury 95 is 7.6e-06. In cover the agreement is exact: every one of the bush rollout's residuals is 0. After 50 rest steps the open-ground agent's injury measured 85.0002 against a predicted 85.0000; the bush agent reached zero injury on step 19 and stayed there.

The rest budget was measured in the same run rather than assumed: nutrition fell by exactly 1.0000 per rest step against a metabolic_cost of 1, with a worst per-step deviation of 0e+00. The claim that a resting agent eats nothing, and therefore that its rest budget is nutrition / metabolic_cost, is confirmed rather than argued.

09 The recommendation, and the rule that produced it

The feasible region of Figure 3 has room in it, so a point inside it has to be chosen rather than found. The rule is stated here because a point picked by eye is not reproducible.

CLAUSE 1
Switch the compounding off
Figure 4 is the evidence. At any base rate large enough to be useful in cover, a positive recovery_accel_rate pushes the open past θ inside the budget.
CLAUSE 2
Anchor the healing rate inside cover to an experiment that already ran
The rest-premium sweep was calibrated so that a 70-point wound closes in about 14 rest steps, at a flat 5 points per step. Making the in-cover rate equal to that keeps the injured window comparable with those runs — base × multiplier = 5.
CLAUSE 3
Both conditions must hold at both budgets, strictly
Not only the 50-step median budget but the 100-step budget of a world that starts at full nutrition — and with strict inequality, so the recommendation does not sit on its own boundary.
CLAUSE 4
Take the weakest intervention that survives
Among the 3 round-number pairs that pass, take the largest base rate, which is the smallest multiplier. A smaller premium is a smaller change to the world.

Recommended setting

body:
  recovery_base_rate: 0.2
  recovery_accel_rate: 0
  recovery_in_bush_multiplier: 25

Read the shipped rows first. Both clear the entire 100-point scale in the open inside either budget, so both fail condition A by the largest margin the scale allows. The recommended row clears 10 points in the open on the median budget and 20 on the full-nutrition budget, against a threshold of 25 — and to clear θ out in the open it would have to rest for 125 consecutive steps, which is 1.25 times the longest budget any shipped world grants and 25% of the whole 500-step episode.

An independent check the design did not ask for

Everything above is about what is possible, not about what an agent would choose. The agent's reward is the reduction in homeostatic drive, the distance of its body state from its setpoints — and resting costs a unit of nutrition, which pushes that distance back up. Taking a typical mid-episode state, injury 70 and nutrition 50, one rest step under the recommended setting is worth -0.42 in the open and +3.40 on a bush. The open-ground rest step is not merely futile, it is punished: the hunger it costs outweighs the injury it clears. That is a separate argument from the definition and it lands in the same place, which is the most reassuring thing on this page.

10 What moves if the thresholds move

θ and the budget are choices. Because condition A depends on them only through their ratio, one table covers both sensitivities: the ratio θ / budget is the largest base rate condition A allows.

The one row that fails is the strictest corner of the space — half the threshold and twice the budget at once. Everywhere else the recommendation holds, and the failure mode is graceful: halve the base rate, double the multiplier, and the in-cover rate is unchanged. On acceleration the tolerance is much tighter and worth stating as numbers: at the recommended base rate the largest workable recovery_accel_rate is 0.033 on the median budget and 0.004 on the full-nutrition budget. At base 0.1 those become 0.055 and 0.016; at base 0.05, 0.076 and 0.027. All of them are between one and two orders of magnitude below the shipped 0.5.

11 Where the analysis design needed correcting

The study was specified before it was run. Six things in that specification turned out to be wrong, incomplete, or true only under a condition that was not stated. They are recorded here rather than quietly fixed, so a reader who remembers the original brief can see what moved.

1. The 50-step budget is not the budget of the shipped default world
The brief derived 50 steps as the median of a start nutrition drawn uniformly from 0 to 100. That draw is real, but only in worlds that switch randomised starting nutrition on. The shipped base configuration does not: it starts every episode at full nutrition, giving a 100-step budget, which is twice as strict. Every figure and table on this page now carries both.
2. The quoted recurrence dropped a term
The brief wrote the injury update as clip(injury - recovery, 0, max_injury). The simulation writes clip(injury + applied_inc - recovery, 0, max_injury), where applied_inc is this step's slice of any damage still being spread over 3 steps. It makes no difference to the undamaged case this study is about, but it hides a real asymmetry: the rest streak keeps climbing during those 3 steps while healing is blocked, so a compounding setting comes out of a hit faster than the clean curve suggests. The conclusion about acceleration is therefore conservative, and the direction of the error is worth knowing.
3. “A resting agent eats nothing” is true only while eating is an action
It holds on every maintained world, because eating is its own action there and resting is a different one. But the simulation also supports worlds where eating happens automatically on contact with food, and in those the flag is a function of the agent's position alone, not of what it chose to do. An agent resting on a food cell in such a world eats every step, and its rest budget is no longer bounded by nutrition at all. The definition should name that assumption.
4. The budget is a fatal bound, which makes the test conservative rather than merely approximate
An agent that really spends nutrition / metabolic_cost steps resting starves on the last one. So the definition grants the open strictly more rest than any surviving agent could take, which means it overstates what the open can heal. A setting that fails condition A under this definition fails it with room to spare. That is a strength of the definition and it was not stated.
5. The definition is about possibility, not about choice
Nothing in it asks whether an agent would take the rest steps it is granted. Under the homeostatic reward the recommended setting makes an open-ground rest step actively negative at a typical mid-episode state (§9), which is a stronger result than the definition claims — and a different one. The two are kept apart on this page rather than merged.
6. Figure 3 cannot show both shipped settings
The brief asked for the two shipped settings to be drawn throughout. Figure 3 is a plane at recovery_accel_rate = 0, and only one of the two shipped settings lives there. Plotting the other one on it would have placed a point at coordinates the setting does not have. It appears in Figures 1, 2 and 4, and its absence from Figure 3 is stated in that figure's caption.

12 What this page does not show

Limitations, stated rather than implied

No agent was trained. This is a tuning study of the environment's arithmetic. Whether an injured agent actually learns to walk to a bush under these settings is the experiment this page exists to make worth running, and it has not been run.

The validation is narrow. Figure 5 is two rollouts of one setting under one seed. It validates the shape of the recurrence and the location premium; a defect that only appears at some other recovery_accel_rate would not be caught.

Adopting the recommendation leaves the inert regime. At exactly 1.0 the in-bush premium is not compiled into the simulation at all, which is what makes today's runs bit-identical to runs that predate the setting. A multiplier of 25 switches that branch on. That is intended, but it means any world adopting these values is a new experiment rather than a continuation of an old one.

The wound and the cover-step count are borrowed. 70 points in 25 rest steps comes from the calibration of an earlier sweep, not from a measurement of what wounds agents actually carry. A measured distribution of injury at the moment agents choose to rest would be a better anchor, and does not exist yet.
